question_text: A company runs nightly SageMaker training jobs on ml.p3.2xlarge instances. Reducing batch size affects convergence not cost.
option_text: Switch to Reserved Instances with a 1-year commitment

question_text: A deep learning model shows high accuracy on the training set but performs significantly worse on the validation set. The gap between training and validation accuracy increases as training continues. What does this pattern indicate and what is the most effective remedy?
explanation: A large and growing gap between training and validation performance is the classic symptom of overfitting — the model has memorized training examples rather than learning generalizable patterns. Adding dropout layers randomly disables neurons during training which prevents co-adaptation and forces the model to learn more robust distributed representations. L1 or L2 regularization penalizes large weights. Underfitting is the opposite pattern where both training and validation performance are poor. Increasing model size makes overfitting worse not better.
option_text: The model is underfitting — increase the number of layers and neurons

question_text: A SageMaker training job is using a large language model with 7 billion parameters. Each parameter requires 4 bytes in float32 format. The team is using ml.p3.8xlarge instances with 4 GPUs each having 16 GB of memory. The model weights alone require approximately 28 GB which exceeds a single GPU's memory. Which distributed training strategy should the ML engineer use?
explanation: Model parallelism is correct when the model itself is too large to fit in a single GPU's memory. The model's layers are split across multiple GPUs — each GPU holds a portion of the model. Data parallelism would not help because each replica of the model still needs to fit on one GPU. Increasing batch size increases memory requirements. Using fp16 (half precision) reduces the 28GB to about 14GB which might fit on a single GPU but model parallelism is the standard solution when the model exceeds GPU memory.
option_text: Use data parallelism to distribute the training data across multiple GPUs

question_text: An ML engineer is building a linear regression model to predict house prices. The model has 200 features and is severely overfitting. The engineer suspects many features are irrelevant. Which regularization technique should be applied to simultaneously reduce overfitting and perform automatic feature selection by driving irrelevant feature weights to exactly zero?
explanation: L1 regularization (Lasso) adds a penalty equal to the absolute value of weights to the loss function. This has the mathematical property of driving some weights to exactly zero which effectively removes the corresponding features from the model. This performs automatic feature selection. L2 regularization (Ridge) shrinks all weights toward zero but never exactly to zero so all features remain in the model. Dropout is a neural network technique not for linear regression. Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving but does not perform feature selection.
option_text: L2 regularization (Ridge)

question_text: A team is training a deep learning model on a large dataset across 8 GPU instances. The model architecture fits on a single GPU but training is slow because only one instance processes data at a time. Which distributed training approach should the ML engineer use to speed up training?
explanation: Data parallelism is correct when the model fits on a single GPU but training needs to be faster by processing more data simultaneously. Each GPU holds a complete copy of the model and trains on a different batch of data. Gradients are synchronized across all GPUs after each step. Model parallelism splits model layers across GPUs which is for when the model does not fit on one GPU — that is not the case here. Increasing batch size alone without distributing does not leverage multiple instances. Sequential training on each GPU one at a time provides no speedup.
option_text: Use model parallelism to split model layers across the 8 GPU instances

question_text: A company fine-tunes a pre-trained image classification model on a proprietary manufacturing defect dataset. After deployment the model performs well on defect classification but its accuracy on the original ImageNet benchmark has dropped significantly compared to the base model. What problem has occurred and what technique addresses it?
explanation: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning on a new task overwrites the weights the model learned during original pre-training causing it to lose performance on the original task. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) addresses this by adding a regularization term that penalizes changes to weights that were important for the original task. Dropout addresses overfitting not catastrophic forgetting. L2 regularization penalizes all large weights equally not specifically weights important to previous tasks. Data augmentation adds variety to training data but does not prevent forgetting.
option_text: Overfitting — apply dropout regularization during fine-tuning

question_text: An ML engineer is running SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with 100 total training jobs and wants to run as many parallel jobs as possible to find the optimal hyperparameters faster. question_text: A team is training a ResNet-50 image classification model on 50000 custom product images. The model reaches 98% training accuracy but only 72% validation accuracy. The gap is large and does not improve after 50 epochs. Which combination most effectively addresses the problem?
explanation: All three techniques address overfitting and together provide the strongest regularization. L2 regularization penalizes large weights reducing model complexity. Dropout randomly disables neurons forcing the model to learn redundant representations. Data augmentation artificially expands the training set with transformed examples teaching the model to be invariant to flips and rotations. The combination of all three is significantly more effective than any single technique because they address overfitting from different angles — weight penalty, neuron co-adaptation, and training data variety.
option_text: Apply only L2 regularization as the primary overfitting solution

question_text: A company wants to deploy a very large BERT-based text classification model to production but the model is 1.2 GB which is too large for the target deployment hardware. The team trains a smaller 3-layer transformer model using the large BERT model's outputs as soft targets instead of the original hard labels. The small model achieves similar accuracy to the large model at one-tenth the size. What technique did the team use?
explanation: Knowledge distillation is the technique where a smaller student model is trained to mimic the output distributions (soft targets) of a larger teacher model. The soft targets contain richer information than hard labels — they encode the relative probabilities the teacher assigns to all classes which helps the student learn the decision boundaries more efficiently. Quantization converts weight precision and does not involve training a separate smaller model. Pruning removes connections from the existing large model rather than training a new small model. Model parallelism is about distributing training across hardware not creating a smaller model.
option_text: Model quantization — converting weights to int8 reduces the model to one-tenth the size

question_text: A company needs to train a large language model (LLM) with 20 billion parameters. The model is too large for any single GPU instance but the training dataset fits entirely in memory. The team is using SageMaker and wants to minimize training time while staying within a GPU memory budget. Which distributed training architecture should the ML engineer design?
explanation: Pipeline parallelism (a form of model parallelism implemented in SageMaker Model Parallel) splits the model's layers across multiple GPU instances into stages. Each stage holds a portion of the model layers. Micro-batches flow through the pipeline with different stages processing different micro-batches simultaneously improving GPU utilization. This directly addresses the model-too-large-for-one-GPU constraint. Data parallelism alone does not solve the memory problem — each worker still needs the full model. Increasing batch size increases memory requirements further. Spot Training without the correct distributed strategy still fails due to memory constraints.
option_text: Use data parallelism across 32 ml.p4d.24xlarge instances

question_text: An ML engineer reviews the training history of a neural network. The training loss curve decreases smoothly. The validation loss curve decreases initially but then increases sharply starting at epoch 20. The gap between training and validation loss grows wider each epoch after that. SageMaker Debugger does not report vanishing or exploding gradients. The team has already applied L2 regularization. Which additional actions are most likely to reduce the overfitting? (Select the BEST single answer)
explanation: The scenario shows classic overfitting with no gradient issues. L2 regularization is already applied. The most effective additional steps are: (1) add dropout to reduce co-adaptation between neurons, (2) collect more training data to give the model more examples to generalize from, and (3) implement early stopping to halt training before validation loss diverges further at epoch 20. These three actions attack overfitting from different angles. Increasing model depth makes overfitting worse. Switching to Bayesian optimization is for hyperparameter search not for addressing an overfitting model. Disabling L2 removes an existing protection.
option_text: Increase model depth and add more neurons to increase learning capacity
